summary:
Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in December 2022, on the strength of a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights program. The Human Dignity Trust records the Barbados case as one of a series of constitutional challenges to colonial-era anti-gay statutes across the Eastern Caribbean, and a High Court ruling on sodomy published in May 2023 found discrimination based on sexual orientation unconstitutional.

Impunity for anti-trans violence is documented and recent enough to matter. In February 2018 Hoffmann was attacked with a meat cleaver by Brandon Coward, suffering serious injuries including to her throat; he was convicted in April 2019 and ordered to pay Hoffmann BDS$460 (US$230) or face three months in prison, an outcome reported through Maurice Tomlinson and the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network in which no jail time was handed down. A visibly trans visitor who is assaulted should not expect a custodial sentence against the attacker.

Employment protection does not reach trans workers. The Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020, passed by Parliament in August 2020, bars discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status, but trans activist Alexa D.V. Hoffmann argues it excludes trans workers because gender identity and gender expression are not listed as protected grounds. Reporting from August 2020 states that trans Barbadians are frequently fired or denied jobs for dressing in a way employers consider wrong.

No same-sex relationship is recognised. In June 2016 the government ruled out changing the law to allow same-sex marriage, and in September 2020 announced only a plan to recognise some form of civil union followed by a referendum on gay marriage; critics called the civil union proposal unnecessarily vague and expected the referendum to fail, and neither had been enacted as of the source's account. In 2018 activists filed a case with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights challenging sections 9 and 12 of the Sexual Offences Act (Ch.154), and the Commission gave the government three months to respond in late July 2019; failure to repeal could send the matter to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights for a binding decision.

Family formation is closed: same-sex couples are unable to legally adopt, surrogacy is illegal although not explicitly prohibited or regulated by law, and same-sex couples are not recognised as families.

Entry rules touch spouses directly. In July 2020 the government's Welcome Stamp remote-work visa initially allowed foreign workers to bring only an opposite-sex spouse, a rule changed to permit same-sex spouses. The government has also questioned the legitimacy of LGBT migration: in 2011 it said it was investigating claims that gay Barbadians were seeking refugee status in Canada, and in 2016 Foreign Minister Maxine McClean expressed concern that such applications were an attempt to abuse the Canadian refugee system, noting that two of nine Canadian applications had been denied.

Two gaps should be weighed alongside these findings. Identity-document processes and legal gender recognition for trans Barbadians are not covered by the available sources, and no findings appear on access to transition-related healthcare, mental health or specialist care.
tangentialFactors:
Official hostility has been stated plainly and repeatedly. In 2016 Attorney General Adriel Brathwaite said Barbados would not change the law to allow same-sex marriage, and after UK Prime Minister David Cameron's 2011 CHOGM warning that aid could be linked to sodomy laws he publicly said Barbados would not be dictated to by the United Kingdom. A government minister warned that external forces were trying to impose same-sex marriage, prompting Human Rights Watch to call the response a cheap political trick since its report did not mention same-sex marriage.

Religious and political pressure runs in both directions. Fundamentalist groups including the New Testament Church have claimed sexual orientation is chosen and argued that discrimination against LGBT people should be encouraged, and human rights activists report that more American evangelical ministers arriving in Barbados have spread homophobic rhetoric more widely. The Barbados Nation newspaper's informal comment line drew opposition to a proposed gay tourism package. The Anglican Bishop of Barbados and the Catholic Church oppose the buggery law while respecting LGBT rights, and Prime Minister Mia Mottley, elected May 2018, is reportedly pro-LGBT.

A 2016 Guyanese newspaper reported over 300 LGBT members in Barbados seeking asylum in Canada, the UK and the US, and UGLAAB said it would investigate the same allegations. The August 2020 commentary contrasts the Welcome Stamp visa's marketing of openness with the anti-gay law then in force.
localsOnly:
Barbados Gays, Lesbians and All-Sexuals Against Discrimination (BGLAD), founded in 2013 by Donnya Piggott and Ro-Ann Mohammed, was set up to create an education mechanism and open public dialogue for the LGBT community. Pride events have served an awareness-raising function, beginning with a small event in November 2017 and a parade of about 120 people on Rihanna Drive, Bridgetown in July 2018.

The second Trans Day of Remembrance vigil was held in Barbados in November 2018, organised with NOW, a local ally and named veteran trans advocates, and included trans activist Alexa Hoffmann's first-person account of visibility and danger on the island. UGLAAB works on AIDS, and the Barbados Fertility Centre offers IVF and artificial insemination to lesbian couples.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights case filed in 2018 proceeded past the government's July 2019 response deadline, and whether any referral to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights followed, is unresolved in the available sources. The September 2020 civil union plan and referendum are likewise reported only as announced; whether either was subsequently enacted or held is not sourced here.

No findings appear on the treatment of LGBT minors, detention of unaccompanied youth, or school-based anti-bullying and gender-affirming education. The only youth-adjacent legal detail available is that under the former Section 12 of the Sexual Offences Act, serious indecency carried a maximum penalty of ten years in prison where the act was committed on or towards a person aged 16 or older. No findings appear on trans-specific custody or parental-rights outcomes.
